text:
Miss Marjoribanks lost her mother when she was only fifteen, and when,
to add to the misfortune, she was absent at school, and could not have
it in her power to soothe her dear mamma's last moments, as she herself
said.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes basic plot premise (mother's death, daughter away at school) with minimal emotional complexity.
enrichment.summary: Miss Marjoribanks lost her mother at fifteen while absent at school, unable to comfort her in her final moments.

context: This opening passage introduces the novel's protagonist, Lucilla Marjoribanks, and the death of her mother that sets the entire plot in motion. It establishes her age (fifteen), her location (away at school), and her subsequent sense of guilt and duty that will drive her decision to return home and dedicate herself to comforting her widowed father—a plan that will form the central conflict of the chapter.

text:
Words are sometimes very poor exponents of such an event: but it
happens now and then, on the other hand, that a plain intimation
expresses too much, and suggests emotion and suffering which, in
reality, have but little, if any, existence. Mrs Marjoribanks, poor
lady, had been an invalid for many years; she had grown a little peevish
in her loneliness, not feeling herself of much account in this world.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Offers narrative commentary on the gap between emotion and expression, establishing Oliphant's ironic mode.
enrichment.best_quote: Words are sometimes very poor exponents of such an event: but it happens now and then, on the other hand, that a plain intimation expresses too much, and suggests emotion and suffering which, in reality, have but little, if any, existence.
enrichment.summary: The narrator reflects that words may either fail to convey genuine sorrow or exaggerate emotion that scarcely existed, introducing Mrs Marjoribanks as a long-suffering invalid.

context: This chunk appears immediately after Miss Marjoribanks loses her mother at age fifteen while away at school. It provides narrative commentary explaining that while her mother's death might seem momentous, Mrs. Marjoribanks had actually been a sickly, neglected invalid for years who felt little value in life. This context undercuts the emotional significance of the loss and establishes that the mother's death was less tragic than it initially appears, setting up the contrast with Lucilla's theatrical grief and romantic notions of filial duty.

text:
There are some rare natures that are content to acquiesce in the general
neglect, and forget themselves when they find themselves forgotten; but
it is unfortunately much more usual to take the plan adopted by Mrs
Marjoribanks, who devoted all her powers, during the last ten years of
her life, to the solacement and care of that poor self which other
people neglected.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extends social critique of self-pity and neglect with Oliphant's characteristic dryness.
enrichment.best_quote: devoted all her powers, during the last ten years of her life, to the solacement and care of that poor self which other people neglected.
enrichment.summary: The narrator observes that Mrs Marjoribanks, unlike rare selfless natures, devoted herself entirely to grieving her own neglect and insignificance.

context: This passage describes Mrs. Marjoribanks's response to being neglected and undervalued as an invalid during her final years. It explains that rather than gracefully accepting neglect, she became self-absorbed and focused on her own comfort, a character trait that will later influence her daughter Lucilla's self-centered approach to her own life and plans.

text:
The consequence was, that when she disappeared from
her sofa—except for the mere physical fact that she was no longer
there—no one, except her maid, whose occupation was gone, could have
found out much difference. Her husband, it is true, who had, somewhere,
hidden deep in some secret corner of his physical organisation, the
remains of a heart, experienced a certain sentiment of sadness when he
re-entered the house from which she had gone away for ever.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine exposition of the household's indifference to Mrs Marjoribanks' death.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Marjoribanks' death changes little in the household; only her maid grieves, and Dr Marjoribanks feels only a faint sadness.

context: This chunk describes the death of Mrs. Marjoribanks and its minimal impact on her household. It follows the narrator's explanation that Mrs. Marjoribanks had spent her final years absorbed in caring for herself rather than being a meaningful presence in her family's life. The passage emphasizes her insignificance—that her death left almost no trace except for the practical loss of her maid's employment. It also introduces Dr. Marjoribanks's subdued emotional response, establishing his character as emotionally reserved and setting up the disconnect between his actual feelings and his daughter Lucilla's dramatic expectations of grief and devotion when she returns home from school.

text:
But Dr
Marjoribanks was too busy a man to waste his feelings on a mere
sentiment. His daughter, however, was only fifteen, and had floods of
tears at her command, as was natural at that age.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces Dr Marjoribanks' character with standard exposition; Lucilla's tears presented as natural.
enrichment.summary: Dr Marjoribanks is too busy to dwell on sentiment, while Lucilla, at fifteen, weeps naturally for her mother.

context: This chunk appears early in the chapter after Mrs. Marjoribanks' death is announced. It contrasts the father's emotional detachment from his wife's passing—he experiences only a "sentiment of sadness" but is too occupied with his medical practice to dwell on it—with the daughter Lucilla's youthful, tearful response to her mother's death. The passage establishes the emotional gulf between the practical, reserved Dr. Marjoribanks and his fifteen-year-old daughter, whose grief is more performative and literature-inspired, setting up the central tension of the chapter.

text:
All the way home she
revolved the situation in her mind, which was considerably enlightened
by novels and popular philosophy—for the lady at the head of Miss
Marjoribanks school was a devoted admirer of  Friends in Council , and
was fond of bestowing that work as a prize, with pencil-marks on the
margin—so that Lucilla's mind had been cultivated, and was brimful of
the best of sentiments.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Characterizes Lucilla's sentimental education and literary influence, hinting at her idealistic nature.
enrichment.best_quote: Lucilla's mind had been cultivated, and was brimful of the best of sentiments.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla's mind has been shaped by popular sentimental literature, especially *Friends in Council*, filling her with noble ideals.

context: Lucilla Marjoribanks is traveling home from school after learning of her mother's death. On her journey, she reflects on her situation, her mind shaped by the sentimental literature and moral philosophy she has been taught, particularly *Friends in Council*. This reading has filled her with idealistic notions about duty and self-sacrifice, which will inform her plans to comfort her widowed father.

text:
She made up her mind on her journey to a great
many virtuous resolutions; for, in such a case as hers, it was
evidently the duty of an only child to devote herself to her father's
comfort, and become the sunshine of his life, as so many young persons
of her age have been known to become in literature. Miss Marjoribanks
had a lively mind, and was capable of grasping all the circumstances of
the situation at a glance.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes Lucilla's core character: dutiful idealism grounded in quick practical intelligence, combining sentimentality with ambition.
enrichment.best_quote: Miss Marjoribanks had a lively mind, and was capable of grasping all the circumstances of the situation at a glance.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla resolves to devote herself to her father's comfort as an only child should, believing she must become the sunshine of his life.

context: Lucilla Marjoribanks, a fifteen-year-old schoolgirl, learns of her mother's death while away at school. On her journey home, she formulates elaborate plans to become a devoted daughter and comfort to her widowed father, inspired by sentimental literature she has read. However, her romantic ideals about filial duty clash with her father's practical temperament and preference for solitude, leading to disappointment when he insists she return to school rather than remain at home.

text:
Thus, between the outbreaks of her tears for
her mother, it became apparent to her that she must sacrifice her own
feelings, and make a cheerful home for papa, and that a great many
changes would be necessary in the household—changes which went so far
as even to extend to the furniture.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's grandiose fantasies of household reform reveal her ambition disguised as filial duty, opening the novel's central irony.
enrichment.best_quote: she must sacrifice her own feelings, and make a cheerful home for papa, and that a great many changes would be necessary in the household—changes which went so far as even to extend to the furniture.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla plans extensive household reforms, including refurbishment, ostensibly to comfort her father but revealing her appetite for management.

context: Lucilla Marjoribanks, traveling home after her mother's death, imaginatively plans how she will become her widowed father's comfort. During her journey, she resolves that she must sacrifice her own feelings to create a cheerful home for him, including making significant household changes such as replacing the furniture.

text:
Miss Marjoribanks sketched to
herself, as she lay back in the corner of the railway carriage, with her
veil down, how she would wind herself up to the duty of presiding at her
papa's dinner-parties, and charming everybody by her good humour, and
brightness, and devotion to his comfort; and how, when it was all over,
she would withdraw and cry her eyes out in her own room, and be found in
the morning languid and worn-out, but always heroical, ready to go
downstairs and assist at dear papa's breakfast, and keep up her smiles
for him till he had gone out to his patients.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's elaborate fantasy of self-sacrifice—weeping in her room then smiling at breakfast—is both comic and psychologically revealing, establishing the novel's pattern of performed emotion.
enrichment.best_quote: how she would wind herself up to the duty of presiding at her papa's dinner-parties, and charming everybody by her good humour, and brightness, and devotion to his comfort; and how, when it was all over, she would withdraw and cry her eyes out in her own room, and be found in the morning languid and worn-out, but always heroical
enrichment.summary: Lucilla fantasizes about presiding at her father's dinner-parties with charming brightness, then retiring to weep privately before resuming her heroic cheerfulness at breakfast.

context: Lucilla Marjoribanks, a fifteen-year-old girl recently informed of her mother's death, travels home by railway carriage. During her journey, she fantasizes about the dutiful, self-sacrificing role she will adopt as a devoted daughter to her widowed father, imagining herself presiding over his dinners with cheerfulness while secretly grieving in private.

text:
Altogether the picture was
a very pretty one; and, considering that a great many young ladies in
deep mourning put force upon their feelings in novels, and maintain a
smile for the benefit of the unobservant male creatures of whom they
have the charge, the idea was not at all extravagant, considering that
Miss Marjoribanks was but fifteen. She was not, however, exactly the
kind of figure for this  mise en scène .

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrative dismissal of Lucilla's literary fantasy; transition to physical description introduces the gap between her self-image and reality.
enrichment.summary: The narrator observes that Lucilla's romantic vision of dutiful grief-stricken beauty does not match her actual appearance.

context: Lucilla Marjoribanks, newly bereaved of her mother at fifteen, fantasizes during her train journey home about her future role as a devoted daughter. She imagines herself presiding over her widowed father's household, sacrificing her own feelings to be his comfort—a vision inspired by sentimental novels and popular philosophy she has read at school. However, the narrator notes this romantic ideal is undermined by Lucilla's actual physical appearance: she is a large, ungainly girl with coarse features, thick tawny curls, and oversized hands and feet—hardly the delicate, ethereal figure such a melodramatic domestic role would require.

text:
When her schoolfellows talked
of her to their friends—for Lucilla was already an important personage
at Mount Pleasant—the most common description they gave her was, that
she was "a large girl"; and there was great truth in the adjective.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes Lucilla's physical distinctiveness; the epithet 'a large girl' marks her as unusual and will be central to her later influence.
enrichment.best_quote: the most common description they gave her was, that she was 'a large girl'
enrichment.summary: Lucilla's schoolfellows describe her as 'a large girl,' emphasizing her substantial, full-bodied appearance.

context: This chunk appears in the physical description of Lucilla Marjoribanks at age fifteen, shortly after she has learned of her mother's death and is traveling home from boarding school at Mount Pleasant. It establishes her substantial physical presence and appearance as she contemplates how she will devote herself to comforting her widowed father.

text:
She
was not to be described as a tall girl—which conveys an altogether
different idea—but she was large in all particulars, full and
well-developed, with somewhat large features, not at all pretty as yet,
though it was known in Mount Pleasant that somebody had said that such a
face might ripen into beauty, and become "grandiose," for anything
anybody could tell.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Detailed physical description distinguishing Lucilla from conventional beauty; introduces the possibility of future 'grandiose' beauty.
enrichment.best_quote: face might ripen into beauty, and become 'grandiose'
enrichment.summary: Lucilla is large but not tall, with robust features not yet pretty but potentially capable of ripening into grandeur.

context: This passage is part of the physical description of Lucilla Marjoribanks at age fifteen, following her mother's death. It appears after schoolfellows describe her as "a large girl" and clarifies the distinction between being large rather than tall, establishing her appearance as she returns home to comfort her widowed father.

text:
Miss Marjoribanks was not vain; but the word had
taken possession of her imagination, as was natural, and solaced her
much when she made the painful discovery that her gloves were half a
number larger, and her shoes a hair-breadth broader, than those of any
of her companions; but the hands and feet were both perfectly well
shaped; and being at the same time well clothed and plump, were much
more presentable and pleasant to look upon than the lean rudimentary
schoolgirl hands with which they were surrounded.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals Lucilla's psychological resilience and vanity; her plump hands and feet are well-formed despite being larger than her schoolfellows'.
enrichment.best_quote: the word had taken possession of her imagination, as was natural, and solaced her much when she made the painful discovery that her gloves were half a number larger, and her shoes a hair-breadth broader, than those of any of her companions
enrichment.summary: Lucilla consoles herself over her larger gloves and shoes by recognizing that her hands and feet, though large, are well-proportioned and well-clothed.

context: This passage describes Miss Lucilla Marjoribanks's physical appearance at school, specifically her hands and feet. It occurs as part of a detailed characterization of her as a large, well-developed girl of fifteen returning home after her mother's death. The chunk illustrates how Lucilla, though not conventionally pretty, compensates for her larger size with good grooming and well-proportioned features, drawing comfort from the concept of her face becoming "grandiose."

text:
To add to these
excellences, Lucilla had a mass of hair which, if it could but have been
cleared a little in its tint, would have been golden, though at present
it was nothing more than tawny, and curly to exasperation.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine physical description of Lucilla's hair and its colour.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla has abundant tawny, curly hair that could be golden if its tint were clearer.

context: This passage describes Lucilla's physical appearance, specifically her hair, as part of a detailed character portrait of the fifteen-year-old girl before she returns home from school following her mother's death. The description emphasizes her large, well-developed figure and features that do not yet meet conventional beauty standards but show promise of future attractiveness.

text:
She wore it
in large thick curls, which did not, however, float or wave, or do any
of the graceful things which curls ought to do; for it had this
aggravating quality, that it would not grow long, but would grow
ridiculously, unmanageably thick, to the admiration of her companions,
but to her own despair, for there was no knowing what to do with those
short but ponderous locks.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended description of Lucilla's problematic hair—thick, short, unmanageable—with mild comic frustration.
enrichment.best_quote: curly to exasperation
enrichment.summary: Lucilla's curls are thick and short rather than long and graceful, a source of exasperation to her despite admiration from companions.

context: This passage appears within Lucilla Marjoribanks's physical description as she returns home from school after her mother's death. The narrator is detailing her appearance—her large frame, features, hands, feet, and hair—establishing that despite being "large" rather than conventionally pretty, she possesses certain qualities that suggest future attractiveness. This particular sentence focuses on her hair texture, emphasizing how its thick, unmanageable curls frustrate Lucilla even as they impress her schoolmates, highlighting the gap between others' perceptions of her and her own self-consciousness about her appearance.

text:
These were the external characteristics of
the girl who was going home to be a comfort to her widowed father, and
meant to sacrifice herself to his happiness. In the course of her rapid
journey she had already settled upon everything that had to be done; or
rather, to speak truly, had rehearsed everything, according to the habit
already acquired by a quick mind, a good deal occupied with itself.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transition to action; establishes Lucilla's habit of mental rehearsal and self-absorption, key to her character.
enrichment.best_quote: had rehearsed everything, according to the habit already acquired by a quick mind, a good deal occupied with itself.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla has mentally settled all details of how she will comfort her father, revealing her habitual self-rehearsal and self-preoccupation.

context: After her mother's death, fifteen-year-old Lucilla Marjoribanks travels home from school, mentally rehearsing the role she plans to play as her widowed father's devoted daughter. This passage concludes the physical description of Lucilla and introduces her elaborate self-directed plan to comfort and sacrifice herself for her father's happiness, which she has already choreographed in detail during her journey home.

text:
First, she meant to fall into her father's arms—forgetting, with that
singular facility for overlooking the peculiarities of others which
belongs to such a character, that Dr Marjoribanks was very little given
to embracing, and that a hasty kiss on her forehead was the warmest
caress he had ever given his daughter—and then to rush up to the
chamber of death and weep over dear mamma.

enrichment.interest_rationale: First action sequence; Lucilla's fantasized embrace with her father reveals her blindness to his character—a source of comedy and subsequent disappointment.
enrichment.best_quote: forgetting, with that singular facility for overlooking the peculiarities of others which belongs to such a character, that Dr Marjoribanks was very little given to embracing, and that a hasty kiss on her forehead was the warmest caress he had ever given his daughter
enrichment.summary: Lucilla plans to fall into her father's arms, unaware that he is cold and not given to embraces, knowing only perfunctory kisses.

context: This chunk describes Lucilla's imagined homecoming upon learning of her mother's death. Still at school when her mother passes, Lucilla has spent her journey home fantasizing about how she will comfort her widowed father through devoted filial sacrifice. The chunk reveals her romanticized expectations of a tearful, emotionally demonstrative reunion—expectations that will be thoroughly disappointed by her father's actual temperament and indifference.

text:
"And to think I was not there
to soothe her last moments!" Lucilla said to herself, with a sob, and
with feelings sufficiently real in their way. After this, the devoted
daughter made up her mind to come downstairs again, pale as death, but
self-controlled, and devote herself to papa. Perhaps, if great emotion
should make him tearless, as such cases had been known, Miss
Marjoribanks would steal into his arms unawares, and so surprise him
into weeping.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's fantasy of weeping over her mother and strategically moving her father to tears; comedy of her misreading his emotions.
enrichment.best_quote: If great emotion should make him tearless, as such cases had been known, Miss Marjoribanks would steal into his arms unawares, and so surprise him into weeping.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla fantasizes weeping over her mother's chamber, then surprising her emotionally restrained father into tears through strategic tenderness.

context: Lucilla is traveling home by railway after learning of her mother's death. She has been mentally rehearsing how she will fulfill her duty as a devoted daughter by comforting her widowed father, imagining the emotional scenes she will perform. This chunk captures her romanticized fantasy of her homecoming, wherein she plans to weep over her mother's body and then devotedly console her father, drawing on literary models of filial sacrifice.

text:
All this went briskly through her mind, undeterred by the
reflection that tears were as much out of the Doctor's way as embraces;
and in this mood she sped swiftly along in the inspiration of her first
sorrow, as she imagined, but in reality to suffer her first
disappointment, which was of a less soothing character than that mild
and manageable grief.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrative irony: Lucilla proceeds unaware that tears are as foreign to her father as embraces; foreshadows her disappointment.
enrichment.best_quote: undeterred by the reflection that tears were as much out of the Doctor's way as embraces; and in this mood she sped swiftly along in the inspiration of her first sorrow, as she imagined, but in reality to suffer her first disappointment
enrichment.summary: The narrator comments that Lucilla travels in her 'first sorrow,' unaware she is actually heading toward her first disappointment.

context: Lucilla has just lost her mother and is traveling home from school, mentally rehearsing the dramatic scenes of grief and filial devotion she plans to enact. This passage marks the transition from her elaborate fantasies to the reality that awaits her—a reality that will disappoint her expectations of becoming her father's comfort through tearful devotion.

text:
When Miss Marjoribanks reached home her mother had been dead for
twenty-four hours; and her father was not at the door to receive her as
she had expected, but by the bedside of a patient in extremity, who
could not consent to go out of the world without the Doctor. This was a
sad reversal of her intentions, but Lucilla was not the woman to be
disconcerted.

enrichment.interest_rationale: First major disappointment: Dr Marjoribanks is absent at a patient's deathbed, thwarting Lucilla's carefully rehearsed scenario.
enrichment.best_quote: her mother had been dead for twenty-four hours; and her father was not at the door to receive her as she had expected, but by the bedside of a patient in extremity, who could not consent to go out of the world without the Doctor. This was a sad reversal of her intentions, but Lucilla was not the woman to be disconcerted.
enrichment.summary: Upon arriving home, Lucilla finds her father absent, attending a dying patient, which reverses her expectations but fails to disconcert her.

context: Lucilla Marjoribanks returns home from school after her mother's death, expecting to find her father at the door and to execute her carefully rehearsed plan of becoming his devoted comfort. However, she discovers he is absent attending to a dying patient, forcing her to adapt her romantic notions of filial duty to reality.

text:
She carried out the second part of her programme without
either interference or sympathy, except from Mrs Marjoribanks's maid,
who had some hopes from the moment of her arrival. "I can't abear to
think as I'm to be parted from you all, miss," sobbed the faithful
attendant. "I've lost the best missus as ever was, and I shouldn't mind
going after her.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla proceeds with her programme alone, comforted by her mother's maid, who grieves genuinely; contrast between the two women's motivations.
enrichment.best_quote: I can't abear to think as I'm to be parted from you all, miss
enrichment.summary: Lucilla carries out her plan to view her mother alone, comforted by the maid, who grieves the loss of her mistress.

context: After her mother's death, Lucilla returns home from school with rehearsed plans to comfort her father. Upon arrival, she finds her father absent attending a patient and proceeds with her intended programme of grief. Ellis, her mother's devoted maid, provides the only sympathy and emotional support during this period, lamenting the loss of her mistress and expressing her own grief over the separation from the household.

text:
Whenever any one gets a good friend in this world,
they're the first to be took away," said the weeping handmaiden, who
naturally saw her own loss in the most vivid light. "Ah, Ellis," cried
Miss Marjoribanks, reposing her sorrow in the arms of this anxious
attendant, "we must try to be a comfort to poor papa!"

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla consoles her mother's maid and extends sympathy, revealing her conventional filial duty.
enrichment.best_quote: Ah, Ellis,
enrichment.summary: Lucilla comforts the maid Ellis, expressing resolve that they must both be a comfort to poor Papa.

context: This passage occurs immediately after Lucilla arrives home from school following her mother's death. Ellis, her mother's devoted maid, expresses her grief over losing her mistress, and Lucilla responds by embracing Ellis and resolving that they must together comfort her father—establishing the central motivation for Lucilla's subsequent plans to devote herself to his care.

text:
With this end Lucilla made herself very troublesome to the sober-minded
Doctor during those few dim days before the faint and daily lessening
shadow of poor Mrs Marjoribanks was removed altogether from the house.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine exposition of the days before Mrs Marjoribanks' burial; Lucilla is troublesome to her father.
enrichment.summary: During the days before her mother's funeral, Lucilla makes herself troublesome to Dr Marjoribanks with her constant attentions.

context: After her mother's death, Lucilla attempts to comfort her father by arranging a fire and tea in his library, but he rejects her efforts harshly. Undeterred by this setback, she continues trying to be helpful to him during the days before the funeral.

text:
When that sad ceremony had taken place, and the Doctor returned, serious
enough, Heaven knows, to the great house, where the faded helpless
woman, who had notwithstanding been his love and his bride in other
days, lay no longer on the familiar sofa, the crisis arrived which Miss
Marjoribanks had rehearsed so often, but after quite a different
fashion. The widower was tearless, indeed, but not from excess of
emotion.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dr Marjoribanks returns home after the funeral to face his daughter; his emotional numbness and introspection introduce tragic depth.
enrichment.best_quote: The widower was tearless, indeed, but not from excess of emotion.
enrichment.summary: Dr Marjoribanks returns home after the funeral, tearless but heavy-hearted, awaiting the emotional scene he anticipates from Lucilla.

context: The Doctor returns home after his wife's funeral. Lucilla has prepared an elaborate emotional scene to comfort him, but finds him unmoved and dismissive of her theatrical gestures of devotion. This passage marks the turning point where his actual response contradicts her carefully rehearsed expectations.

text:
On the contrary, a painful heaviness possessed him when he
became aware how little real sorrow was in his mind, and how small an
actual loss was this loss of his wife, which bulked before the world as
an event of just as much magnitude as the loss, for example, which poor
Mr Lake, the drawing-master, was at the same moment suffering.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dr Marjoribanks' inner realization that his wife left little mark on the world; profound meditation on her insignificance and their loveless marriage.
enrichment.best_quote: a painful heaviness possessed him when he became aware how little real sorrow was in his mind, and how small an actual loss was this loss of his wife, which bulked before the world as an event of just as much magnitude as the loss, for example, which poor Mr Lake, the drawing-master, was at the same moment suffering.
enrichment.summary: Dr Marjoribanks feels a painful heaviness realizing that his wife's death is truly no real loss to him, though the world treats it as significant.

context: Doctor Marjoribanks experiences a crisis of conscience after his wife's funeral. Rather than feeling overwhelming grief, he discovers he feels little real sorrow at her death, recognizing the gap between the world's perception of his loss and his actual emotional experience. This realization troubles him, as he acknowledges that his wife's passing has left minimal impact on his life or feelings.

text:
It was
even sad, in another point of view, to think of a human creature passing
out of the world, and leaving so little trace that she had ever been
there. As for the pretty creature whom Dr Marjoribanks had married, she
had vanished into thin air years and years ago. These thoughts were
heavy enough—perhaps even more overwhelming than that grief which
develops love to its highest point of intensity.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Continuation of Dr Marjoribanks' introspection: the woman he married has vanished; his grief is not romantic love but existential heaviness.
enrichment.best_quote: It was even sad, in another point of view, to think of a human creature passing out of the world, and leaving so little trace that she had ever been there. As for the pretty creature whom Dr Marjoribanks had married, she had vanished into thin air years and years ago.
enrichment.summary: Dr Marjoribanks reflects sadly that his wife, the pretty woman he once married, vanished long ago, and now she leaves the world with scarcely a trace.

context: This passage reflects Dr. Marjoribanks's private meditations on his wife's death. Rather than experiencing intense grief, he contemplates the melancholy fact that his wife left little mark on the world during her life, and that the woman he once married had emotionally withdrawn years before her physical death. These are his honest, somewhat detached thoughts as he processes his loss in the library after the funeral.

text:
But such were not
precisely the kind of reflections which could be solaced by paternal
 attendrissement  over a weeping and devoted daughter.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrator notes that Dr Marjoribanks' reflections are too heavy for paternal comfort-seeking; establishes the ironic distance between father and daughter.
enrichment.summary: These philosophical reflections would not be soothed by Lucilla's tearful devotion, creating an unbridgeable gap between parent and child.

context: The Doctor has just returned home after his wife's funeral. Rather than feeling profound grief, he experiences a heavy melancholy about how little trace his wife left on the world and how the woman he once married has long since vanished. This reflection cannot be comforted by his daughter's emotional devotion and tears.

text:
It was May, and
the weather was warm for the season; but Lucilla had caused the fire to
be lighted in the large gloomy library where Dr Marjoribanks always sat
in the evenings, with the idea that it would be "a comfort" to him;
and, for the same reason, she had ordered tea to be served there,
instead of the dinner, for which her father, as she imagined, could have
little appetite.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's well-intentioned but misguided efforts to comfort her father reveal her lack of understanding of his nature; sets up the central comic conflict.
enrichment.best_quote: Lucilla had caused the fire to be lighted in the large gloomy library where Dr Marjoribanks always sat in the evenings, with the idea that it would be 'a comfort' to him; and, for the same reason, she had ordered tea to be served there, instead of the dinner, for which her father, as she imagined, could have little appetite.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla lights a fire and serves tea in her father's library on a warm May evening, believing these will comfort him in his grief.

peremptory father; "I never had any doubt on that subject. You can stay
over Sunday and rest yourself. Monday or Tuesday will be time enough to
go back to Mount Pleasant; and now you had better ring the bell, and get
somebody to bring you something—or I'll see to that when I go
downstairs. It's getting late, and this has been a fatiguing day.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dr Marjoribanks confirms Lucilla will return to school; she can stay until Monday or Tuesday.
enrichment.summary: Dr Marjoribanks peremptorily insists Lucilla return to Mount Pleasant by Monday or Tuesday.

context: Dr. Marjoribanks firmly dismisses his daughter Lucilla's tearful plea to remain at home as his comfort following her mother's death. After she has emotionally thrown herself at his feet vowing to sacrifice everything for him, he calmly but decisively tells her she must return to school, allowing her only a few days to rest. This moment represents Lucilla's first major disappointment, as her carefully rehearsed plan to become her widowed father's devoted companion is rejected by a man who values his solitude and independent habits over filial sentiment.

text:
I'll
send you up some negus, and I think you had better go to bed."

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dr Marjoribanks sends Lucilla to bed with negus; practical, dismissive conclusion to their encounter.
enrichment.summary: Dr Marjoribanks orders Lucilla to take some negus and retire to bed after the fatiguing day.

context: Dr Marjoribanks dismisses his daughter Lucilla after she has emotionally pleaded to stay home and be a comfort to him following her mother's death. Despite her theatrical display of devotion and willingness to sacrifice herself, he firmly insists she return to school, offering her refreshment and bed as a way to end their conversation and assert his authority.

text:
And with these commonplace words, Dr Marjoribanks withdrew in calm
possession of the field. As for Lucilla, she obeyed him, and betook
herself to her own room, and swallowed her negus with a sense, not only
of defeat, but of disappointment and mortification which was very
unpleasant.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla obeys and retires with disappointment and mortification; the narrator emphasizes her defeat and her feelings of loss.
enrichment.best_quote: she obeyed him, and betook herself to her own room, and swallowed her negus with a sense, not only of defeat, but of disappointment and mortification which was very unpleasant.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla obeys and withdraws, experiencing acute mortification and disappointment rather than the triumph she had anticipated.

context: Dr. Marjoribanks refuses his daughter's offer to stay home and be a comfort to him after her mother's death, insisting she return to school. Lucilla, who had rehearsed an elaborate plan of self-sacrifice and devotion, is forced to accept his decision despite her disappointment.

text:
To go back again and be an ordinary schoolgirl, after the
pomp and woe in which she had come away, was naturally a painful
thought; she who had ordered her mourning to be made long, and
contemplated new furniture in the drawing-room, and expected to be
mistress of her father's house, not to speak of the still dearer
privilege of being a comfort to him; and now, after all, her active mind
was to be condemned over again to verbs and chromatic scales, though she
felt within herself capacities so much more extended.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's reflection on her defeat: she must return to school as an ordinary girl, abandoning her fantasies of household management and being her father's comfort.
enrichment.best_quote: To go back again and be an ordinary schoolgirl, after the pomp and woe in which she had come away, was naturally a painful thought; she who had ordered her mourning to be made long, and contemplated new furniture in the drawing-room, and expected to be mistress of her father's house, not to speak of the still dearer privilege of being a comfort to him; and now, after all, her active mind was to be condemned over again to verbs and chromatic scales, though she felt within herself capacities so much more extended.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla reflects bitterly that she must return to school as an ordinary girl, abandoning her visions of household management and being her father's comfort.

context: Lucilla's disappointed reaction after her father refuses her offer to stay home and care for him following her mother's death. Having rehearsed an elaborate fantasy of becoming his devoted companion and mistress of the household, she must instead return to school, a humiliating return to ordinary schoolgirl life that she feels beneath her newfound sense of maturity and expanded capabilities.

text:
Miss Marjoribanks
did not by any means learn by this defeat to take the characters of the
other personæ in her little drama into consideration, when she rehearsed
her pet scenes hereafter—for that is a knowledge slowly acquired—but
she was wise enough to know when resistance was futile; and like most
people of lively imagination, she had a power of submitting to
circumstances when it became impossible to change them.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator reflects that Lucilla learns the lesson not to consider others' characters, but she is pragmatic enough to submit when resistance is futile.
enrichment.best_quote: she was wise enough to know when resistance was futile; and like most people of lively imagination, she had a power of submitting to circumstances when it became impossible to change them.
enrichment.summary: The narrator notes that Lucilla does not learn from defeat to consider others' characters, but she knows how to submit to inevitable circumstances.

context: After her mother's death, fifteen-year-old Lucilla Marjoribanks returns home determined to sacrifice herself for her father's comfort, having rehearsed an elaborate program of devoted daughterhood. However, Dr. Marjoribanks firmly rejects her offer, insisting she return to school and that he prefers to be left alone. This chunk reflects Lucilla's response to this unexpected defeat: while she doesn't learn to consider others' actual characters and motivations, she demonstrates pragmatic flexibility by accepting the impossible situation and postponing her grand plans for taking charge of the household.

text:
Thus she
consented to postpone her reign, if not with a good grace, yet still
without foolish resistance, and retired with the full honours of war. She had already rearranged all the details, and settled upon all the
means possible of preparing herself for what she called the charge of
the establishment when her final emancipation took place, before she
returned to school.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla accepts defeat 'with the full honours of war'; she immediately begins planning her future reign and arranging her education to manage the household.
enrichment.best_quote: She had already rearranged all the details, and settled upon all the means possible of preparing herself for what she called the charge of the establishment when her final emancipation took place, before she returned to school.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla accepts her defeat with strategic grace, already planning how to prepare herself to manage the household when she finally comes of age.

context: After her father refuses to let her stay home to comfort him and insists she return to school, Lucilla accepts his decision without further resistance, though with disappointment. Rather than being truly defeated, she uses her remaining time at home to plan how she will eventually take charge of the household and become indispensable to her father once she is old enough. She approaches her return to school as a period of preparation for her future role as mistress of his house.

text:
"Papa thought me too young," she said, when she
reached Mount Pleasant, "though it was dreadful to come away and leave
him alone with only the servants; but, dear Miss Martha, you will let me
learn all about political economy and things, to help me manage
everything; for now that dear mamma is gone, there is nobody but me to
be a comfort to papa."

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's narrative at school reframes her defeat as sacrifice; she persuades her headmistress to direct her education toward household management and 'political economy.'
enrichment.best_quote: Papa thought me too young, though it was dreadful to come away and leave him alone with only the servants; but, dear Miss Martha, you will let me learn all about political economy and things, to help me manage everything; for now that dear mamma is gone, there is nobody but me to be a comfort to papa.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla tells her headmistress that she needs to study political economy to eventually manage her father's household and be a comfort to him.

context: This passage occurs at the very end of the chapter, after Lucilla has returned to Mount Pleasant School following her mother's death and her father's rejection of her offer to stay home and comfort him. Despite her disappointment at being sent back to school, Lucilla reframes the situation to her headmistress Miss Martha, claiming her father thought her too young while strategically securing permission to study political economy and household management. She has already achieved the visible marker of womanhood through her long mourning dress, and now uses this moment to direct her own education toward her ultimate goal of becoming mistress of her father's household.

text:
And by this means Miss Marjoribanks managed to influence the excellent
woman who believed in  Friends in Council , and to direct the future
tenor of her own education; while, at least, in that one moment of
opportunity, she had achieved long dresses, which was a visible mark of
womanhood, and a step which could not be retraced.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Final paragraph: Lucilla successfully influences her headmistress to redirect her education; she has secured long dresses and the foundation of her future influence. A decisive triumph disguised as modest acceptance.
enrichment.best_quote: by this means Miss Marjoribanks managed to influence the excellent woman who believed in Friends in Council, and to direct the future tenor of her own education; while, at least, in that one moment of opportunity, she had achieved long dresses, which was a visible mark of womanhood, and a step which could not be retraced.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla successfully persuades her headmistress to teach her household management; she also achieves the long dresses that mark her passage to womanhood.

context: Lucilla Marjoribanks returns home after her mother's death determined to become a comfort to her widowed father and take charge of the household. Her father, Dr. Marjoribanks, firmly rejects her offers of devotion and insists she return to school, disappointing her plans. Accepting this defeat, Lucilla strategically uses her return to Mount Pleasant to influence her headmistress into directing her education toward domestic management, while securing the symbolic achievement of wearing long mourning dresses—a mark of womanhood that represents her first victory in her larger ambitions to eventually preside over her father's household.

text:
Dr Marjoribanks was so far from feeling the lack of his daughter's
powers of consolation, that he kept her at Mount Pleasant for three
years longer, during which time it is to be supposed he managed to be
comfortable after a benighted fashion—good enough for a man of fifty,
who had come to an end of his illusions.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Sets up the Doctor's domestic situation after Lucilla's departure—routine expository context establishing he manages adequately despite lacking female presence.
enrichment.best_quote: good enough for a man of fifty, who had come to an end of his illusions
enrichment.summary: The Doctor keeps Lucilla at school for three years, managing his household adequately if somewhat sparely without her presence.

context: This opening paragraph introduces Dr. Marjoribanks's contentment during his daughter Lucilla's three-year absence at boarding school, establishing that despite lacking a female presence in his household, he manages well with good dinners and domestic order—setting up the later revelation of his daughter's ambitions to revolutionize Carlingford society upon her return home.

text:
To be sure, there were in the
world, and even in Carlingford, kind women, who would not have objected
to take charge of the Doctor and his "establishment," and be a comfort
to him; but, on the whole, it was undeniable that he managed tolerably
well in external matters, and gave very good men's dinners, and kept
everything in perfect order, so far as it went.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces the social interest in the Doctor's unmarried status and hints at the competitive marriage market, with gentle satirical commentary on women's designs.
enrichment.summary: Kind women in Carlingford would gladly marry the Doctor, but he manages his household well and his good dinners are appreciated by the men of the community.

context: Dr. Marjoribanks has been without his daughter Lucilla for three years. This passage describes how he has managed his household during her absence, noting that while various women in Carlingford would have been willing to take charge of his domestic affairs, he has proven capable of maintaining good order and hosting excellent dinners through his own efforts and his cook's skill.

text:
Naturally the fairer
part of existence was left out altogether in that grim, though
well-ordered house; but then he was only a man and a doctor, and knew no
better; and while the feminine part of Grange Lane regarded him with
natural pity, not only for what he lacked, but for a still more sad
defect, his total want of perception on the subject, their husbands and
fathers rather liked to dine with the Doctor, and brought home accounts
of sauces which were enough to drive any woman to despair.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Satirical commentary on gender and domestic management—the contrast between what women and men value in the Doctor is mildly amusing and thematically relevant to the novel's interest in society and propriety.
enrichment.summary: Women pity the Doctor for his lack of domestic refinement, but men enjoy his excellent dinners, suggesting divided values between the sexes in provincial society.

context: Dr. Marjoribanks has managed his household without his daughter Lucilla for three years following her mother's death. Though the "fairer part of existence" is absent from his grim but orderly home, he maintains excellent dinners that earn him social approval from the men of Grange Lane, while the women pity his domestic deficiencies and lack of awareness about them.

text:
Some of the
ladies of Grange Lane—Mrs Chiley, for example, who was fond of good
living herself, and liked, as she said, "a little variety"—laid siege
to the Doctor, and did their best to coax his receipts out of him; but
Dr Marjoribanks knew better than that.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine exposition establishing the competitive social interest in the Doctor's table and introducing minor characters.
enrichment.summary: Ladies of Grange Lane, including Mrs Chiley, attempt to gain the Doctor's culinary secrets but are unsuccessful.

context: Dr. Marjoribanks has managed his household well for three years without his daughter Lucilla's help, earning a reputation for excellent dinners. Local ladies of Grange Lane, including Mrs. Chiley, attempt to obtain his cooking recipes, but he refuses to divulge them, instead crediting his skilled cook.

text:
He gave all the credit to his
cook, like a man of sense; and as that functionary was known in
Carlingford to be utterly regardless and unprincipled in respect to
gravy-beef, and the materials for "stock," or "consommé," as some people
called it, society was disinclined to exert its ordinary arts to seduce
so great an artiste from the kitchen of her indulgent master. And then
there were other ladies who took a different tone.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces the cook as a valued character and shows the Doctor's sensibility, with mild satire on society's respect for culinary talent and the cook's disreputable sourcing practices.
enrichment.summary: The Doctor credits his cook with the dinners' success, and society respects her too much to attempt seduction because of her dubious procurement methods.

context: Dr. Marjoribanks has remained a widower for three years, managing his household and hosting excellent dinners that have earned him renown in Carlingford society. While some ladies have attempted to coax his cook's recipes from him, the doctor credits his cook for the dinners' success. The cook's questionable sourcing practices and reputation as a skilled artiste make her difficult to poach. Other ladies in society disapprove of the doctor's focus on dining rather than more serious domestic concerns.

text:
"Dr Marjoribanks,
poor man, has nothing but his table to take up his mind," said Mrs
Centum, who had six children; "I never heard that the heart could be
nourished upon sauces, for my part; and for a man who has his children's
future to think of, I must say I am surprised at you, Mr Centum." As
for young Mrs Woodburn, her reply was still more decisive, though milder
in its tone. "Poor cook!

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces moralizing criticism of the Doctor through Mrs Centum and provides characterization of her through free indirect discourse, with mild satirical effect.
enrichment.best_quote: I never heard that the heart could be nourished upon sauces, for my part
enrichment.summary: Mrs Centum judges the Doctor harshly for focusing on his table rather than his children's future, establishing her as a moralistic voice.

context: This chunk represents a turning point in the chapter's discussion of Dr. Marjoribanks's social standing in Carlingford. After the narrator describes how the Doctor's excellent dinners have made him unrivalled in Grange Lane, various women of the community offer their judgments on his lifestyle. Mrs. Centum, a mother of six children, criticizes him for focusing excessively on his table rather than on more serious domestic concerns, while Mrs. Woodburn begins to voice sympathy for his overworked cook. These contrasting female perspectives highlight the social commentary surrounding the Doctor's domestic arrangements and foreshadow the community's expectations for change upon his daughter Lucilla's return home.

text:
I am so sorry for her," said the gentle young
matron.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces young Mrs Woodburn's gentle criticism through a very brief speech—routine social commentary establishing another perspective on the Doctor's priorities.
enrichment.best_quote: Poor cook!
enrichment.summary: Young Mrs Woodburn expresses sympathy for the cook rather than criticism of the Doctor.

context: Young Mrs Woodburn expresses sympathy for Dr Marjoribanks's overworked cook, arguing that the Doctor's focus on elaborate dinners neglects his domestic responsibilities and places unreasonable demands on his kitchen staff.

text:
"You know you always like something for breakfast, Charles; and
then there is the children's dinner, and our lunch, and the servants'
dinner, so that the poor thing is worn out before she comes to what
 you  call the great event of the day; and you know how angry you were
when I asked for a kitchen-maid for her, poor soul." The consequence of
all this was, that Dr Marjoribanks remained unrivalled in Grange Lane in
this respect at least.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Woodburn's gentle speech is more characterizing than critical, showing her sympathetic nature through dialogue that indirectly critiques her husband's behavior and the demands on servants.
enrichment.best_quote: You know you always like something for breakfast, Charles; and then there is the children's dinner, and our lunch, and the servants' dinner, so that the poor thing is worn out before she comes to what you call the great event of the day
enrichment.summary: Mrs Woodburn sympathetically explains to her husband that the cook is exhausted by daily household demands before attending to special dinners.

context: Young Mrs Woodburn defends Dr Marjoribanks's cook against criticism from other ladies in Grange Lane who covet his culinary secrets, arguing that the cook is overworked managing multiple daily meals and deserves sympathy rather than being seduced away from the Doctor's service. This defense explains why Dr Marjoribanks maintains his unrivalled reputation for excellent dinners in the neighborhood.

text:
When rumours arose in Carlingford of a possible
second marriage for the Doctor—and such rumours naturally arose three
or four times in the course of the three years—the men of Grange Lane
said, "Heaven forbid!" "No wife in the world could replace Nancy," said
Colonel Chiley, after that fervent aspiration, "and none could put up
with her;" while, on the other side, there were curious speculations
afloat as to the effect upon the house, and especially the table, of the
daughter's return.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes the Doctor's unmarried status as a topic of social speculation and introduces the idea that his dinners might change with a new mistress—relevant to plot anticipation.
enrichment.best_quote: No wife in the world could replace Nancy, and none could put up with her
enrichment.summary: Marriage rumors circulate about the Doctor, but men prefer him unmarried, while women speculate about how his daughter's return might affect his household management.

context: Dr. Marjoribanks has remained a widower for three years, managing his household and earning acclaim for his excellent dinners prepared by his cook Nancy. The community of Carlingford speculates about a potential second marriage for the Doctor, with men praising Nancy's irreplaceability while women wonder how his daughter Lucilla's return home will affect the household's operations.

text:
When a young woman comes to be eighteen it is
difficult to keep her at school; and though the Doctor had staved off
the danger for the moment, by sending Lucilla off along with one of her
schoolfellows, whose family was going abroad, to make orthodox
acquaintance with all the Swiss mountains, and all the Italian capitals,
still that was plainly an expedient for the moment; and a new mistress
to the house, which had got along so well without any mistress, was
inevitable.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes the necessity of Lucilla's return from school and hints at the anticipatory energy her arrival will generate, advancing plot setup toward her return home.
enrichment.summary: The Doctor sends Lucilla abroad as a delaying tactic, but her return to assume her role as mistress of the house is inevitable.

context: This chunk discusses the practical necessity of Lucilla's return home from school as she reaches eighteen years old. The Doctor's decision to send her abroad to Switzerland and Italy is presented as a temporary measure to delay the inevitable moment when she must assume her role as mistress of the household in Carlingford, following three years of her absence during which her father's domestic arrangements have functioned smoothly under the cook Nancy's management.

text:
So that it cannot be denied Miss Marjoribanks's advent was
regarded in Carlingford with as much interest and curiosity as she could
have wished.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Signals the novel's central concern with Lucilla's impact on Carlingford society; her arrival is established as a matter of municipal importance and high anticipation.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla's return is awaited with great interest and curiosity in Carlingford society.

context: The chunk appears at paragraph [P10], marking the transition from discussion of Dr. Marjoribanks's three years managing his household alone to Lucilla's return home as an eighteen-year-old. It emphasizes that her homecoming has become a matter of significant public interest in Carlingford, as the townspeople eagerly anticipate how this determined and energetic young woman will influence local society and particularly her father's famous dinner table.

text:
For it was already known that the Doctor's daughter was not
a mild young lady, easy to be controlled; but, on the contrary, had all
the energy and determination to have her own way, which naturally
belonged to a girl who possessed a considerable chin, and a mouth which
could shut, and tightly curling tawny tresses, which were still more
determined than she was to be arranged only according to their
inclination.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Physical characterization of Lucilla establishes her determined, assertive nature through vivid physical description that signals her personality—strong Dickinsian-style character introduction.
enrichment.best_quote: had all the energy and determination to have her own way, which naturally belonged to a girl who possessed a considerable chin, and a mouth which could shut, and tightly curling tawny tresses, which were still more determined than she was to be arranged only according to their inclination
enrichment.summary: Lucilla is known to be strong-willed and assertive, with facial features that express her determination.

context: This passage appears in paragraph P11 and describes Lucilla Marjoribanks's reputation in Carlingford society as she prepares to return home from school at age eighteen. The chunk characterizes her as a determined, headstrong young woman with distinctive physical features that reflect her strong-willed personality, establishing her as someone not easily managed—a key trait that will shape her ambitious plans to revolutionize local society.

text:
It was even vaguely reported that some passages-of-arms had
occurred between Miss Marjoribanks and the redoubtable Nancy during the
short and uncertain opportunities which were afforded by holidays; and
the community, accordingly, regarded as an affair of almost municipal
importance Lucilla's final return home.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes conflict between Lucilla and Nancy, and frames her return as an affair of social importance, building anticipation and establishing her as a disrupter.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla has had conflicts with Nancy during holidays, and her final return is regarded as a matter of significant community interest.

context: This passage appears midway through the opening chapter, after establishing Dr. Marjoribanks's well-ordered but austere household managed by his cook Nancy during his daughter Lucilla's three-year absence at school. The chunk reflects Carlingford society's anticipation of Lucilla's return home at age eighteen, having heard rumors of conflicts between the strong-willed young woman and Nancy during school holidays. The community views her homecoming with intense curiosity, uncertain whether she will disrupt or enhance the Doctor's famous dinners and social standing.

text:
As for the young lady herself, though she was at school, she was
conscious of having had a career not without importance, even during
these three years of pupilage. Since the day when she began to read
political economy with Miss Martha Blount, who, though the second
sister, was the directing spirit of the establishment, Lucilla had
exercised a certain influence upon the school itself which was very
satisfactory.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces Lucilla's intellectual life and influence on her school community, establishing her as ambitious and capable of exercising power—core characterization for understanding her later project.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla has already exercised considerable influence over her school during her studies, particularly under Miss Martha Blount's guidance in political economy.

context: This chunk appears early in the chapter and marks a transition from describing Dr. Marjoribanks's life during his daughter's three-year absence at school to introducing Lucilla herself upon her impending return to Carlingford. It establishes that despite being away at Mount Pleasant school, Lucilla has already developed a reputation for exercising influence and authority, foreshadowing her plans to reorganize society in her hometown.

text:
Perhaps her course might be a little deficient in grace,
but grace, after all, is but a secondary quality; and, at all events,
Miss Marjoribanks went straight forward, leaving an unquestionable wake
behind her, and running down with indifference the little skiffs in her
way. She was possessed by nature of that kind of egotism, or rather
egoism, which is predestined to impress itself, by its perfect reality
and good faith, upon the surrounding world.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Profound character analysis of Lucilla's personality and method—her egoism, her single-minded pursuit of her aims, and her indifference to those who resist her. This is essential to understanding her as a character.
enrichment.best_quote: Miss Marjoribanks went straight forward, leaving an unquestionable wake behind her, and running down with indifference the little skiffs in her way
enrichment.summary: Lucilla possesses a profound, unself-conscious egoism that impresses itself on others through its complete sincerity and lack of self-doubt.

context: This passage describes Lucilla Marjoribanks's character and personality during her three years at school. It characterizes her as a determined, self-assured young woman driven by complete conviction in her own importance. The narrator explains how her unwavering egotism—combined with genuine belief in herself—allows her to influence those around her, despite her lack of social grace. This characterization establishes the foundation for her ambition to revolutionize society in her hometown of Carlingford upon her return.

text:
There are people who talk of
themselves, and think of themselves, as it were, under protest, and with
depreciation, not actually able to convince themselves that anybody
cares; but Lucilla, for her part, had the calmest and most profound
conviction that, when she discussed her own doings and plans and
clevernesses, she was bringing forward the subject most interesting to
her audience as well as to herself. Such a conviction is never without
its fruits.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Continues deep psychological analysis of Lucilla's egoism and its social effects, distinguishing her from those who are self-deprecating. This is crucial to understanding her power and the novel's central theme.
enrichment.best_quote: Lucilla, for her part, had the calmest and most profound conviction that, when she discussed her own doings and plans and clevernesses, she was bringing forward the subject most interesting to her audience as well as to herself
enrichment.summary: Lucilla's complete conviction in her own importance is the source of her persuasiveness; she genuinely believes her interests are everyone's interests.

context: This chunk appears in a passage describing Lucilla Marjoribanks's character and personality during her time at school, specifically illustrating her supreme self-confidence and egotism. It comes after an introduction to her influential role at Mount Pleasant school and serves as a key characterization of her absolute conviction in her own importance and ability to captivate others through discussion of herself. This trait is presented as foundational to her future success as a leader of society in Carlingford, which is her stated ambition upon returning home after completing her education abroad.

text:
To be sure, there were always one or two independent spirits
who revolted; but for the crowd, it soon became impressed with a
profound belief in the creed which Miss Marjoribanks supported so
firmly. This conviction of the importance and value of her own
proceedings made Lucilla, as she grew older, a copious and amusing
conversationalist—a rank which few people who are indifferent to, or do
not believe in, themselves can attain to.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Completes the analysis of Lucilla's psychological power, showing how her conviction shapes her social influence and conversational gifts—important for understanding her method.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla's profound belief in her own importance makes her an amusing and engaging conversationalist, a quality that few who doubt themselves can achieve.

context: This passage describes Lucilla's narcissistic personality and her ability to convince others of her self-importance through persuasive conversation. It illustrates how her unwavering belief in her own significance naturally impressed itself upon those around her at school, making her an engaging and influential conversationalist despite her lack of modesty or self-doubt.

text:
One thing she had made up her
mind to as soon as she should return home, and that was to revolutionise
society in Carlingford.

enrichment.interest_rationale: States Lucilla's central ambition—to revolutionize Carlingford society—which is the plot's driving force. This is a key revelatory moment establishing her mission.
enrichment.best_quote: One thing she had made up her mind to as soon as she should return home, and that was to revolutionise society in Carlingford
enrichment.summary: Lucilla has decided to revolutionize Carlingford society upon her return home.

context: Lucilla Marjoribanks, the Doctor's eighteen-year-old daughter returning home from school after three years abroad, is introduced as an ambitious and self-assured young woman determined to transform the social life of her provincial town.

text:
On the whole, she was pleased with the success
of the Doctor's dinners, though a little piqued to think that they owed
nothing to herself; but Lucilla, whose instinct of government was of the
true despotic order, and who had no objection to stoop, if by that means
she could conquer, had no such designs against Nancy as were attributed
to her by the expectant audience in Carlingford.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals Lucilla's pragmatic approach to power—she will not contest Nancy's position but will use her as a tool, showing Machiavellian intelligence in her ambitions.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla appreciates the Doctor's successful dinners and will cooperate with Nancy as a prime minister of household affairs, showing her instinct for governance.

context: This chunk appears in the middle section of the chapter where the narrative shifts from describing Dr. Marjoribanks's successful household management after his daughter's departure to introducing Lucilla's impending return home at age eighteen. The chunk reveals Lucilla's pragmatic character and her strategic plans to lead Carlingford society, clarifying that despite rumors, she intends to work with—not against—Nancy, the cook, as part of her scheme to reorganize local social life through her father's dinner table.

text:
On the contrary, she
was quite as much disposed as her father was to take Nancy for
prime-minister; for Miss Marjoribanks, though too much occupied with
herself to divine the characteristic points of other people, had a
sensible and thorough belief in those superficial general truths which
most minds acquiesce in, without taking the trouble to believe.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Shows Lucilla's pragmatic understanding of superficial truths about people, establishing her as intelligent but lacking true psychological penetration—a limitation that will shape the novel.
